title: Fifteen federations, one memorandum: unorganised sector social security
author: Editorial Desk
summary: A 32-member delegation led by Surendra Kumar Pandey met the Union Labour Minister in November 2025.
body:
*Photo: BMS delegation of fifteen federations meets the Labour Minister*

In early November 2025, a **32-member delegation** representing **fifteen all-India unorganised sector federations** affiliated with BMS met the Union Minister for Labour and Employment, **Dr Mansukh Mandaviya**, in New Delhi. According to the BMS website, which carried the report on 8 November 2025, the delegation was led by **Shri Surendra Kumar Pandey**, then the All India Deputy General Secretary of BMS. This post looks at the meeting, at why the unorganised sector is central to the Indian labour question, and at what the federations are asking for.

## Why the unorganised sector matters

Most of India's workers do not have a formal employer, a written contract or a regular wage slip. They work on construction sites, in beedi rolling, on farms, in fishing boats, in forests, in homes, on the roadside and in small workshops. They are the majority of the workforce, yet for a long time they remained outside the reach of most labour protection and social security. Their problems are not the same as those of a factory worker. A construction labourer may change contractor every few months; a beedi roller works at home and is paid by the piece; a fisherman's income depends on the season and the weather. A scheme designed for a factory, with monthly salary deductions, does not fit these cases, which is why each sector needs its own approach.

The Ministry of Labour and Employment's release on the implementation of the Labour Codes says that social security coverage has risen from about 19 per cent of the workforce in 2015 to over 64 per cent in 2025. Whatever the exact method of counting, the figures indicate how large the gap was and how much of it has still to be closed.

## What happened at the meeting

The BMS report says that, in response to the demands raised by the fifteen unorganised sector federations, the Minister stated that the Government is fully committed to extending social security coverage to all workers of the unorganised sector, and that it is the Government's top priority. The delegation presented sector-wise demands, and, as reported on the website, several photographs and press notes were issued after the meeting. The report in its short form on the website does not set out each federation's individual demands, and this post does not attempt to list them in detail.

## What the federations asked for

The federations cover sectors such as construction, beedi, agriculture, fisheries and forest workers. As in earlier BMS memoranda, the common themes of such demands are well known and are summarised below.

- **Registration of every worker.** A worker who is not registered cannot be reached by any scheme. Registration is the first step to everything else.
- **Welfare boards or schemes for each sector.** The needs of a head-load worker, a fisherman and a beedi roller differ, and each sector needs its own board or scheme, financed in a way that suits it.
- **Pension and health cover.** An unorganised worker who works for forty years usually has no pension. Health care costs are the biggest cause of debt among poor families.
- **Skill training and tools.** For artisans and small producers, a better tool or a short course can raise income directly.
- **Speedy rules under the Social Security Code.** The Code sets out the framework, but benefits depend on the rules and schemes framed under it.

## The legal framework behind the demand

The **Code on Social Security, 2020** is the law that matters most here. According to the Government's description, it extends coverage to unorganised, gig, platform and migrant workers, and it defines gig worker, platform worker and aggregator for the first time. Aggregators are to contribute 1 to 2 per cent of their annual turnover into a social security fund, capped at 5 per cent of what they pay these workers. Workers register on the **e-Shram** portal and receive an Aadhaar-linked unique identity, which is intended to make benefits portable when they move between jobs, platforms or States. The benefits that may be notified include life and disability cover, health and maternity benefits, pension, accident insurance and crèche facilities. As Free Press Journal's report on the Codes explains, the national registry is also intended to support skill development and welfare delivery.

BMS has been pressing for this law. At its Kendriya Karya Samiti meeting in Bhopal on 22 to 24 August 2025, it called for the immediate implementation of the Wage Code and the Social Security Code, which it described as more beneficial to ordinary workers than the older laws, and asked for the Indian Labour Conference, which last met in 2015, to be convened. At the same time, BMS kept its objections to some provisions of the Industrial Relations Code and the OSH Code.

## Why this meeting mattered

The meeting showed the organisational pattern of BMS: **sector federations bring concrete issues**, and the central leadership carries them to the Government. A national union is only as strong as its sector bodies, since they know whether a particular scheme is working in a particular district. It also came less than two weeks before the Labour Codes were brought into force on 21 November 2025, at a time when the rules for the Social Security Code were the immediate subject of discussion. A request made at that point has a better chance of influencing how schemes are designed.

## What to watch in the follow-up

A meeting is not a result. The real test will be whether the schemes announced reach the worker. The practical questions are as follows.

1. Will the rules under the Social Security Code provide for sector-specific schemes, or a general scheme only?
2. How will workers with no employer be registered, and who will help those who cannot use a digital portal?
3. Will the funds for welfare come from stable sources, and will they be used for the purposes stated?
4. Will the existing welfare boards, such as those for construction workers, be preserved and strengthened, or will their role change?
5. How will the benefits be made known in villages and in the languages of the workers?

For the federations, the next step is to take the minister's assurance to the districts. This means organising registration camps, helping members with documents, and tracking whether benefits are actually received. A promise of priority becomes meaningful only when a worker in a remote area can show a registration card and receive a benefit in return.

## Closing thought

The unorganised worker builds houses, rolls beedis, grows food, catches fish and gathers forest produce, yet is often the last in line for a benefit. If the Government's statement that social security for this group is its top priority is to be real, the evidence will be in the rules, the schemes and the registrations of the coming months. BMS has said that it will keep following the matter.
